steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our object-centric learning paper, where we use image augmentation to train slot manipulation so object representations become interpretably controllable. Cover the motivation, the problems with earlier controllable-slot approaches, our two main ideas (interpretable controllability and sustainability), and how we evaluate them.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Compositional scene understanding and object-centric learning (OCL)
2. Limits of prior interpretable/controllable object representations; sustainability
3. Our approach to interpretable controllability via image augmentation
4. Sustainability: AIM and SCLoss
5. Experiments overview

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. OCL background
- compositional comprehension of visual scenes (cite) -> needed for localization (cite), reasoning (cite); requires human-like understanding of complex world (cite)
- -> OCL active research area (cite)
- OCL: decompose image into objects, learn their representations (slots), no human-annotated labels

2. Problem with prior work
- interpretable, controllable object representation studied (cite)
- limitation: extra processes to figure out how to interact with slots: manual exhaustive search linking slot values to object properties; feature selector trained on ground-truth properties (Fig. 1 (a))
- cause: training-inference discrepancy, slot interaction only at inference -> ambiguity, hinders interpretable controllability
- second challenge: representation must stay intact after multiple human manipulations
- concept of sustainability: preserve nature of slots, iterative manipulation (Fig. 4 and 5)

3. Interpretable controllability
- advance OCL re interpretability of object representation
- manipulate object representation via human interpretable instructions, self-supervised
- fix discrepancy: image augmentation in training pipeline (Fig. 1 (c))
- slot manipulation in training -> streamlined slot interaction at inference (Fig. 1 (b) and (d))

4. Sustainability
- Auxiliary Identity Manipulation (AIM) + Slot Consistency Loss (SCLoss)
- AIM: learn multi-round manipulation; auxiliary manipulation in intermediate stage, no semantic change (e.g. zero-pixel translations); two rounds = one instruction from augmentation + one auxiliary
- SCLoss: reversible manipulation, e.g. move object 1 pixel right vs 1 pixel left
- -> consistent, reusable representations, multiple modifications, better usability
- AIM + SCLoss -> sustainability

5. Experiments
- interpretable and sustainable controllability
- interpretability: object manipulation with semantically interpretable instructions
- sustainability: novel experiments incl. durability test
- pixel space (image editing via object manipulation) + slot space (property prediction)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Compositional comprehension of visual scenes is essential for many computer vision tasks like localization and reasoning, and it requires a human-like understanding of the complex world. Because of this, object-centric learning (OCL) has become an active research area. The aim of OCL is to make a model decompose an image into objects and learn their representations, called slots, without any human-annotated labels.

To get a deeper understanding of images, interpretable and controllable object representation has been studied. But the previous approaches have limitations in getting interpretable controllability, because they need additional processes to figure out how to interact with slots. For example, they explore the connection between specific values in slots and object properties by a manual exhaustive search, or they train a feature selector with ground-truth object properties (Fig. 1 (a)). The issue comes from a training-inference discrepancy, where interaction with slots is only considered at the inference stage. This discrepancy makes it ambiguous how to interact with object representations, and this hinders interpretable controllability. There is also another challenge that comes after learning interpretable controllability: the object representation should stay intact even after humans manipulate it multiple times. So we come up with the concept of sustainability, which is about the ability to preserve the nature of slots so that they can be manipulated iteratively; see Fig. 4 and 5 for the earlier motivation.

- advance OCL re interpretability of object representation
- manipulate object representation via human interpretable instructions, self-supervised

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Compositional comprehension of visual scenes is essential for many computer vision tasks like localization and reasoning, and it requires a human-like understanding of the complex world. Because of this, object-centric learning (OCL) has become an active research area. The aim of OCL is to make a model decompose an image into objects and learn their representations, called slots, without any human-annotated labels.

To get a deeper understanding of images, interpretable and controllable object representation has been studied. But the previous approaches have limitations in getting interpretable controllability, because they need additional processes to figure out how to interact with slots. For example, they explore the connection between specific values in slots and object properties by a manual exhaustive search, or they train a feature selector with ground-truth object properties (Fig. 1 (a)). The issue comes from a training-inference discrepancy, where interaction with slots is only considered at the inference stage. This discrepancy makes it ambiguous how to interact with object representations, and this hinders interpretable controllability. There is also another challenge that comes after learning interpretable controllability: the object representation should stay intact even after humans manipulate it multiple times. So we come up with the concept of sustainability, which is about the ability to preserve the nature of slots so that they can be manipulated iteratively; see Fig. 4 and 5 for the earlier motivation.

In this work, we advance OCL with respect to the interpretability of object representation. For interpretable controllability, we propose a method that lets us manipulate object representation with human interpretable instructions in a self-supervised manner. We deal with the training-inference discrepancy by adding image augmentation to our training pipeline (Fig. 1 (c)). Since slot manipulation is now part of training, the discrepancy is resolved and the way to interact with slots at inference is streamlined (Fig. 1 (b) and (d)).

Second, to get sustainability in object representation, we introduce Auxiliary Identity Manipulation (AIM) and Slot Consistency Loss (SCLoss). AIM is a method to help the model learn the concept of multi-round manipulation. It is implemented by adding an auxiliary manipulation process in the intermediate stage of slot manipulation, and the auxiliary manipulation does not make any semantic changes to object properties, for example zero-pixel translations. This simple auxiliary process exposes our model to multi-round manipulation: we can do two-round manipulations, one instruction from the augmentation and the other from the auxiliary manipulation. SCLoss lets our model learn the concept of reversible manipulation, like the relationship between moving an object 1 pixel to the right and moving it 1 pixel to the left. When it is trained with SCLoss, our model gives consistent and reusable representations that can go through multiple modifications, which makes them more usable. With AIM and SCLoss, our model gets sustainability in object representation.

We show extensive experiments to demonstrate that our model has interpretable and sustainable controllability. For interpretability, we do object manipulation experiments where slots are guided by semantically interpretable instructions. For sustainability, we introduce novel experiments, including the durability test. Our evaluation covers pixel space assessments like image editing via object manipulation and also slot space analyses like property prediction, so that our approach is examined comprehensively.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Compositional comprehension of visual scenes [1,2,3], essential for various computer vision tasks such as localization [4] and reasoning [5], requires a human-like understanding of the complex world [6,7,8]. In response, object-centric learning (OCL) has emerged as an active research area [9,10,11]. OCL aims to enable a model to decompose an image into objects and to acquire their representations, slots, without human-annotated labels.

In pursuit of a deeper understanding of images, interpretable and controllable object representation has been studied [12,13,14]. Nevertheless, previous approaches face limitations in achieving interpretable controllability, as they require additional processes to figure out how to interact with slots, such as exploring the connection between specific values in slots and object properties by manual exhaustive search, or training a feature selector with ground-truth object properties (Fig. 1 (a)). This issue arises from a training-inference discrepancy, wherein interaction with slots is only considered at the inference stage. The discrepancy brings ambiguity in how to interact with object representations, hindering interpretable controllability. Furthermore, learning interpretable controllability is followed by another challenge: object representation should remain intact even after multiple manipulations by humans. In this context, we devise the concept of sustainability, the ability to preserve the nature of slots so as to allow iterative manipulations; we refer to Fig. 4 and 5 for the earlier motivation.

In this work, we advance OCL with respect to the interpretability of object representation. To achieve interpretable controllability, we propose a method that enables the manipulation of object representation through human interpretable instructions in a self-supervised manner. We address the training-inference discrepancy by incorporating image augmentation into our training pipeline (Fig. 1 (c)). By involving slot manipulation in training, we resolve the discrepancy and streamline the way to interact with slots at the inference stage (Fig. 1 (b) and (d)).

Second, to attain sustainability in object representation, we introduce Auxiliary Identity Manipulation (AIM) and Slot Consistency Loss (SCLoss). AIM is designed to facilitate learning the concept of multi-round manipulation. It is implemented by incorporating an auxiliary manipulation process into the intermediate stage of slot manipulation, where the auxiliary manipulation introduces no semantic change to object properties, such as zero-pixel translations. This simple auxiliary process exposes our model to multi-round manipulation: we can make two-round manipulations, with one instruction from the augmentation and the other from the auxiliary manipulation. Additionally, SCLoss allows our model to learn the concept of reversible manipulation, such as the relationship between moving an object 1 pixel to the right and moving it 1 pixel to the left. Trained with SCLoss, our model produces consistent and reusable representations that can undergo multiple modifications, enhancing their usability. With AIM and SCLoss, our model achieves sustainability in object representation.

Extensive experiments demonstrate the interpretable and sustainable controllability of our model. To assess interpretability, we conduct object manipulation experiments where slots are guided by semantically interpretable instructions. To evaluate sustainability, we introduce novel experiments, including the durability test. Our evaluation covers not only pixel space assessments such as image editing via object manipulation, but also slot space analyses such as property prediction, providing a comprehensive examination of our approach.
